lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 6, Session 2
lesson.footer: Persuasive Speeches | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 6 Session 2

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LY09 comprehension strategies to evaluate a spoken text; VC2E5LA01 language that signals social roles (a child speaking to world leaders); VC2E5LY02 spoken texts using features of voice
plan.shape: listen, map, try: students watch the selected section of Severn's speech, map her message, audience and think-feel-do, then write their own 'who I am and why I care' opening
plan.criticalFeature: a speaker earns the right to be heard by saying who they are and why it matters to them; Severn turns 'only a child' into her strength
decisionPoints: the Why should we listen? round
the choice check: the opening that earns the right to be heard
the exit board: a new credibility line
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Say it. Today: who I am and why I care.
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 1? Say: speeches are written for the ear. Play the clip again; the Worksheet starts from the speech itself.

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: map Severn's speech, judge credibility lines, write lines that earn the right to speak, then your own opening.
resources.title: Severn's Six Minutes
resources.subtitle: Who is she? Why should the world listen?

example.prompt: Any speech: message, audience, think, feel, do.
steps: Message: the big idea in one sentence
Audience: who is in the room?
Think, feel, do: what does she want?
example.answer: Message: adults must stop harming the planet.

items.prompt: Fill in the listening grid for Severn's speech.
rows: What she wants them to think
What she wants them to feel
What she wants them to do
answers: Her message in one sentence
Adults must stop damaging the planet our generation will inherit.
Her audience
world leaders at the 1992 Earth Summit
What she wants them to think
children see the harm clearly
What she wants them to feel
ashamed, responsible, moved
What she wants them to do
stop breaking what they can't fix; act now

example.prompt: 'I'm a lifeguard, and I've pulled plastic from this beach every summer.'
steps: What have they seen or done?
example.answer: Experience: they've seen the problem first-hand.

items.prompt: Topic: a school garden. Which opening earns the right to be heard?
options: I'm Lily. I eat lunch by that dirt patch daily.
I'm Lily. I'm great at speeches.
items.explain: It shows she knows the problem first-hand.

items.prompt: Max opened his speech like this. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Hello, my name is Max and today I am going to do my speech.
items.answer: It says nothing about why we should listen. Fix: I'm Max, and I walk past our flooded oval every winter.

example.prompt: Speaker: a Year 6 student. Issue: climate.
steps: What is your link to the issue?
example.answer: I'm only twelve. But I'll live with your choices longer than anyone here.

items.prompt: Write a line that earns the right to be heard.
rows: a new student: a buddy bench
a kid: a bike path, to the council
answers: a Prep student: more shade
I'm only small, but I get burnt every lunch.
a new student: a buddy bench
I was new here once. I know what it's like to sit alone.
a kid: a bike path, to the council
I'm not old enough to vote, but I ride this road every day.

example.answer: I'm a Year 6 student. I've read about the Arctic all term. And I can't unsee it.

items.prompt: Write the opening of a speech on your issue that tells the audience who you are and why you care.
items.answer: Who they are, their link to the issue, and why it matters, in short spoken sentences.

resources.tip: Finished? Add Severn to your Toolkit, then grab the Extension.

resources.title: Then and Now

steps: What does it do to the audience?
example.answer: It makes the adults feel responsible.

items.prompt: Name three of Severn's techniques and their effect.
answers: a child's point of view
the adults feel responsible
simple, direct requests
it sounds obvious and fair
speaking for future generations
the audience thinks beyond today

steps: End with her kind of request
example.answer: We're still asking. The ice is still melting. Please, stop breaking it.

items.answer: Lines in her plain, direct voice with a current fact and a request.

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: a twelve-year-old once silenced a room of world leaders. Today we find out how.

Cue the selected section of Severn Cullis-Suzuki's Earth Summit speech from the DCE Speech Collection. Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Toolkits out.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning how a speaker earns the right to be heard.
successCriteria: I can say a speaker's message and audience.
I can explain how a speaker shows who they are and why they care.
I can write an opening that earns my right to be heard.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today a twelve-year-old teaches us how to make adults listen.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we all start.
The second one is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 is reachable for all; SC2 is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 is the stretch.

slides.title: A kid at the world's biggest meeting
lines: Rio de Janeiro, 1992. The Earth Summit.
World leaders in the room. A 12-year-old at the microphone.

notes.answer: open - most say no, kids aren't taken seriously
beats: SAY: In 1992,
leaders from around the world met in Rio to talk about the planet.
One speaker was Severn Cullis-Suzuki. She was twelve.
ASK: Would world leaders listen to a twelve-year-old?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: mostly down or sideways
ASK: What would a kid have to do to make them listen?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: say something true; make them feel guilty; be brave
SAY: Let's watch, and find out what she did.
trap: Fix: say that is exactly the doubt Severn used.
notes.prep: Launch sets the context. SOURCES: Severn Cullis-Suzuki, UN Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro, June 1992, aged 12.

slides.meaning: The reasons an audience should believe and listen to you.
slides.example: A lifeguard talking about beach safety has credibility.

notes.answer: the reasons an audience should believe and listen to you
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Credibility. Say it with me. Credibility.
SAY: The reasons an audience should believe and listen to you.
SAY: A lifeguard talking about beach safety has credibility.
ASK: Who has more credibility on school lunches:
a chef or a student who eats them?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: both, for different reasons
trap: thinking credibility only comes from being an adult or an expert.
Fix: ask what has this person seen or lived? That counts too.
notes.prep: The technique word for the session: Toolkit row 2.

rows: Adults must stop harming the planet.
world leaders at the Earth Summit
stop breaking what you can't fix

notes.answer: message, audience, and what she wants them to think, feel and do
beats: PLAY the selected section from the DCE Speech Collection.
SAY: Listen for who she says she is, and who she's talking to.
POINT to Message.
SAY: One sentence for the whole speech. Adults must stop harming the planet.
POINT to Feel.
SAY: She doesn't shout. She makes a room of adults feel responsible.
That's credibility from being a child.
ASK: What does she want them to DO?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: stop breaking it; change; act
trap: writing the topic (the environment) as the message.
Fix: ask what does she want to happen? Student writes a claim.
notes.stretch: Find where she turns being young into a strength.
notes.prep: The model: the listening grid used for every speaker this week. Critical feature: earning the right to be heard. CARE: discuss gently that some students feel worried about the planet.

slides.title: Think, feel or do?
slides.pivot: ask: is it a fact, a feeling or an action?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which word told you?

items.text: Please turn off one light tonight.
Imagine a hungry bear on melting ice.
Arctic summer ice shrinks about 12 percent a decade.
Look at your own children. They are counting on you.

say: Speakers want us to think, feel, then do.
trap: Fix: ask is it a fact? Then it's think.
notes.stretch: Find a line that does two jobs.
notes.help: Look for Please: that's usually do.
notes.prep: Guided practice on the listening grid's last three rows. SC1.

visual.text: "If you don't know how to fix it, please stop breaking it!"

notes.answer: simple logic, a polite word, and a request any child could make
beats: READ it aloud, slowly, the way she said it.
SAY: Twelve words. A child could say it.
POINT to please.
SAY: She's polite, even when she's telling adults off. That makes it hard to argue with.
ASK: Say the line with me, the way she said it.
3 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: If you don't know how to fix it, please stop breaking it!
ASK: Why is this line so hard to argue with?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: it's obvious; it's fair; a kid said it
trap: thinking a powerful line needs big words.
Fix: count the long words. None. Simple is strong.
notes.stretch: Write your own twelve-word line for your issue.
notes.help: Copy her pattern: If you ___, please ___.
notes.prep: A short, famous line for close study; play it in context from the DCE clip. Toolkit row 2: who I am and why I care.

slides.title: Why should we listen?
slides.pivot: ask: what has this person seen, done or lived?
slides.followUp: cold call one board: is that a strong reason to listen?

items.text: I've swum at this beach every morning for ten years.
I'm a Year 6 student, and I'll live with these choices the longest.
items.expect: it affects them; they'll live with it

items.text: I'm a nurse, and I treat sunburnt kids every summer.
items.expect: they're an expert or they've seen it

items.text: I'm only ten. But I can count the bins that overflow every Friday.
items.answer: turns 'only ten' into a strength: they've seen it
items.expect: a weakness made into a strength

say: Each speaker gives a reason to listen.
Write what gives them the right to be heard.
trap: Fix: ask what do they know that we don't? Student rewrites.
notes.stretch: Rank the four by how much you'd trust them.
notes.help: Choose from: experience, expert, it affects them.

slides.title: Which opening earns the right to be heard?
slides.prompt: Topic: our school needs a crossing guard.

options.text: Hi everyone, my name is Jai.
options.misconception: a name is not a reason to listen

options.text: I'm Jai, and I'm really good at talking.
options.misconception: boasting about the speech, not the issue

options.text: I'm Jai, and I cross that busy road twice a day.

notes.answer: C - he lives the problem every day
beats: SAY: Three openings for the same speech. Which makes you listen?
ASK: Which opening earns the right to be heard?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to C
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: what would make B work?
Less -> ask what does each tell us about the issue? re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: C. He crosses that road. He knows. Now we listen.
trap: pointing to A because speeches start with your name.
Fix: say your name is fine, but add why you should be heard.
notes.prep: Decision point before writing. Under 80% means the class builds one opening together on the board.

slides.title: Earn the right to be heard
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish with a speech opening that tells your audience who you are and why you care. Add Severn to your Toolkit.
slides.visualLabel: Who I am and why I care

notes.answer: an opening with who they are and their link to the issue
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Your issue, your opening. Make them believe you before you give one reason.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: why should they listen to YOU about this?
ASK: Read your opening to your partner. Would they listen?
60 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first, then swap.
EXPECT: a real link to the issue
trap: an opening that only gives a name and a topic.
Fix: student adds one thing they've seen, done or lived.
notes.stretch: Extension: name Severn's techniques, then write what she might say today.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, a first line done, a frame.
notes.prep: Independent application. Toolkit row 2 filled in before the exit. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a credibility opening for the student's own speech

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: You're giving a speech to the council asking for a skate park.
Write one line that earns your right to be heard.

notes.answer: e.g. I skate in the car park because there's nowhere else to go
beats: SAY: A new speech, a new audience. Earn their attention.
ASK: Write one line that earns your right to be heard.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a link to the issue: experience, stake or expertise
RECORD who writes only a name. Tomorrow's warm-up.
trap: Hi, I'm ___ and I like skating.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new speech. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: What did Severn do that you could use in your own speech?

notes.answer: open - say who I am and why it matters to me
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can earn the right to be heard?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: What did Severn do that you could use in your own speech?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: say who I am and why it matters to me
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Toolkit row 2 filled. SC2.
